items.text: Country diary: Which tree sounds the best in the wind? Take a bough, the poplar | Derek Niemann
items.article: Frome, Somerset: With a sway and a swoosh, we’re entering the season to enjoy psithurism – the aural quality of the breeze in the trees Frome, Somerset: With a sway and a swoosh, we’re entering the season to enjoy psithurism – the aural quality of the breeze in the trees T he wind-catchers along the bottom of the valley miss nothing. Even the lightest breath has them whispering. And when the wind strengthens, they do a good imitation of the river streaming over boulders below their feet. Truly, when it blows, it pours. Pass a poplar and you are enjoying the best example of psithurism, the sound of wind in trees. All this growing season, I have listened politely to oaks, alders and willows, but if I rocked up in a pub looking for chatty company, I’d want a poplar on the bar stool next to me. The name psithurism seems to have been conjured up from Greek roots as recently as the 19th century, yet the practice is as old as humanity. It exposes a curious and inescapable fact – wind itself has no voice. The explorer‑conservationist John Muir tramped many a mile through America’s wild lands, observing that “winds are advertisements of what they touch”. He may well have been thinking of talkative, animated aspens, but all members of the poplar clan are physiologically equipped to shoot the breeze with a wide range of sound and movement.
